nameStory: The 'dark-green' in this moss's name refers to its distinctive deep, almost blackish-green color that becomes more pronounced when dry. The 'bristle' part comes from the hair-like structures (called peristome teeth) that ring the opening of its spore capsules, looking like tiny bristles under magnification. When the capsules open to release spores, these bristles create a delicate fringe around the opening.
description: Dark-green Bristle Moss is a small cushion-forming moss that grows in compact, rounded tufts. Each tuft is typically only about half an inch to an inch across, made up of densely packed tiny stems with overlapping leaves. The whole plant has a distinctive dark green to blackish-green color that makes it stand out from other mosses. Like other bristle mosses, it produces small, egg-shaped spore capsules on short stalks that emerge from the cushions.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Deep dark green to almost blackish-green color, especially when dry - much darker than most other small mosses you'll encounter

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms tight, compact cushions or small rounded tufts, each about the size of a dime to quarter

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny leaves that overlap like shingles and curl inward when dry, giving the cushions a slightly twisted appearance

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Small egg-shaped capsules on very short stalks, often partially hidden within the leaf cushions, with bristle-like teeth around the opening

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels crisp and slightly rough when dry, becoming softer and more pliable when moistened

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly on tree bark, particularly favoring rough-barked trees like oak and maple

habitat: Dark-green Bristle Moss grows exclusively on the bark of trees, particularly those with rough, furrowed bark like oaks, maples, and ash trees. It prefers the lower trunks of mature trees in mixed hardwood forests and forest edges. You're most likely to spot it in areas with moderate shade and good air circulation, often alongside other small bark-dwelling mosses and lichens.

seasonality.spring: Cushions begin to green up and expand as moisture returns. Spore capsules may be developing but are often still immature and hidden within the leaf clusters.
seasonality.summer: Plants are at their most active growth phase when consistently moist. The dark green color is most apparent during dry spells between rains.
seasonality.fall: Spore capsules mature and become most visible, extending slightly above the cushions on their short stalks. Color remains consistently dark.
seasonality.winter: Cushions contract and become very dark, almost black when frozen. Plants enter dormancy but remain visible and identifiable by their distinctive color and growth form.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, Dark-green Bristle Moss can survive being completely dried out for months at a time, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet - a process it can repeat hundreds of times throughout its lifetime without any damage to its cells.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small cushion mosses on bark, but the distinctively dark, almost blackish-green color sets it apart - most other bark mosses are brighter green, yellow-green, or grayish. Remember: if it's growing on bark and looks almost black-green when dry, it's probably Dark-green Bristle Moss.
contextualKnowledge: This moss was recently moved from the genus Orthotrichum to the newer genus Lewinskya based on DNA studies, so you may still find it listed under its old scientific name Orthotrichum sordidum in older field guides. The species name 'sordida' means 'dirty' in Latin, referring to its dark, somewhat dingy appearance compared to brighter mosses.
compareHints: Dark-green Bristle Moss differs from its relative Showy Bristle Moss by being much darker in color and forming smaller, more compact cushions. Showy Bristle Moss is typically brighter green with a more yellow tint and forms larger, looser tufts. The 'showy' species also tends to have more prominent spore capsules that extend well above the leaves, while Dark-green Bristle Moss keeps its capsules tucked closer to the cushion.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Dark-green Bristle Moss, Showy Bristle Moss typically forms more compact, rounded cushions and has more prominent bristles on its capsules.
